ai.title: Web standard session limit and model ID list added
ai.summary: Three new constants land in common/src/constants/freebuff-models.ts: FREEBUFF_WEB_STANDARD_SESSION_LIMIT, FREEBUFF_WEB_STANDARD_SESSION_RESET_TIMEZONE, and FREEBUFF_WEB_STANDARD_SESSION_PERIOD, which together cap fresh Freebuff Web/Cloud sessions to six per user for full-access models outside the premium/referral pools. A companion definition, FREEBUFF_WEB_STANDARD_MODEL_IDS, freezes the filtered list of non-premium model IDs drawn from FREEBUFF_WEB_ALL_MODELS so browser surfaces share the browser-only standard daily pool. The CLI keeps full-access Web/Cloud models unlimited; only browser surfaces enforce the cap, and the diff adds no reader of the new constants yet.
ai.evidence: common/src/constants/freebuff-models.ts adds `FREEBUFF_WEB_STANDARD_SESSION_LIMIT = 6`, `FREEBUFF_WEB_STANDARD_SESSION_RESET_TIMEZONE`, and `FREEBUFF_WEB_STANDARD_SESSION_PERIOD` constants, and defines `FREEBUFF_WEB_STANDARD_MODEL_IDS` as the frozen list of non-premium model IDs filtered from `FREEBUFF_WEB_ALL_MODELS`. The new session-limit comment and the standard-pool comment accompany these, and no other file in the diff reads them.

entries.summary: Agent Runtime changes across 1 file(s) (+57/−51).

ai.title: Context-pruner subagent lifecycle events
ai.summary: Refined `onResponseChunk` handling in `spawn-agent-inline.ts`. Context-pruner subagents now suppress raw text summaries while forwarding `subagent_start` and `subagent_finish` lifecycle events to the client. This prevents UI noise during internal pruning while maintaining visibility into the pause duration. Uses `sendSubagentChunk` for text and `writeToClient` for lifecycle objects.

eli5.text: When the assistant briefly pauses to trim away old conversation history behind the scenes, that internal step no longer floods your view with a chunk of plain-text summary. You still see a clear marker that the pause started and finished, so the interface can explain why nothing appeared to be happening. This only affects what you see during that pruning pause; all other assistant actions remain exactly as before.

eli5.text: The team quietly swapped out a piece of the assistant's language-handling software for a newer version of the same tool, replacing some of its custom error-handling code with the newer tool's built-in version. If you looked at the surface, nothing about how the assistant responds today would feel different, but behind the scenes it is now relying on the newer library's way of translating error responses instead of its own. This is the kind of maintenance you only notice when it goes wrong, not when it goes right.
